reels.title: One front door for every model

beats.say: Twelve teams, three AI providers, and nobody knows who spent forty thousand dollars last weekend. Sound familiar?
Think of a hotel. Guests do not each get a key to the kitchen. They call the front desk, which knows who they are, what they may order, and keeps the bill.

chip.text: One bill, one set of rules

beats.say: An LLM gateway is that desk. Every team calls it instead of the providers. It holds the secret keys, checks each team's budget, and writes down what every call cost.
And when one kitchen closes, the desk sends the order to another, so the guest still eats.

check.q: Why put a gateway in front of AI models?
opts: One place for keys, budgets, fallbacks and cost records
It makes every model answer more accurately
It lets each team pick its own secret keys
check.why: The gateway handles the rules every team needs once, instead of twelve copies in twelve codebases.

work: List every service that calls a model provider directly today.
Find out who would notice if one team spent ten times its usual amount.

reels.title: First token, then the rest

beats.say: Why does an AI answer start after a pause, then stream quickly? Two different phases.
First, prefill. The server reads your whole prompt at once, in parallel. A three thousand token prompt takes a few hundred milliseconds. That wait is the time to first token.
Then decode. Each new token needs a full pass that reads every weight from memory. At fifty tokens a second, a three hundred token answer takes six more seconds.
So stream the answer. The user feels only the first token, and shorter prompts and caching shrink that wait.

check.q: What mostly sets the time to first token?
opts: Queueing and prefill of the prompt
The number of output tokens
The temperature setting
check.why: The first token waits for the whole prompt to be processed; output length sets the time after that.

work: Measure p95 time to first token for one AI feature.
Check whether the feature streams its answers.

reels.title: What one request costs

beats.say: A support assistant gets two hundred thousand requests a day. What does that cost? Let us do the sum.

Three thousand input tokens at three dollars a million is nine tenths of a cent. Three hundred output tokens at fifteen dollars a million is under half a cent. Together, about one point three five cents.
Cache the fixed two thousand token prefix and it drops to about eight tenths of a cent. Route seven in ten easy requests to a small model and the day falls to about six hundred forty dollars.
Every lever needs an eval run before and after, because cheaper answers can quietly be worse answers.

check.q: Which change lowers cost without touching answer quality, if done right?
opts: Caching a stable prompt prefix
Routing to a smaller model
Cutting the retrieved context in half
check.why: A cached prefix is the same text processed once; routing and trimming context can both change answers.

work: Work out cost per request for one feature you know.
Move the fixed part of a prompt to the start so it can be cached.

reels.title: The KV cache and long context

beats.say: Why does a long conversation cost so much more than a short one? Memory.
While writing, the model keeps keys and values for every earlier token, in every layer, in GPU memory. For a seventy billion parameter model, that is about a third of a megabyte per token.
A thirty two thousand token conversation holds about ten gigabytes. Fewer conversations fit on a GPU, so throughput falls and the price rises.

show.title: GB of KV cache per conversation

beats.say: That is why retrieving the right three thousand tokens usually beats pasting in a hundred thousand.

check.q: Why does long context reduce how many users a GPU can serve?
opts: Its KV cache takes GPU memory per token
The model weights grow with each prompt
Long prompts need a larger model
check.why: The weights are fixed; the cache grows with every token in flight and crowds out other requests.

work: Check the average prompt length of your heaviest feature.
Try trimming retrieved context and rerun the eval set.

reels.title: Batching, quantization and their trade-offs

beats.say: One GPU, one user, one token at a time? That wastes almost all of it.
Each decode step reads all the weights. Reading them once for fifty users costs nearly the same as for one. Continuous batching adds and removes requests at every step.
The catch: each user sees slightly slower tokens, and a full server queues new requests. Operators cap the batch size to hold a latency target.
Quantization stores weights in eight or four bits. Less to read means faster and cheaper, but check quality on your own eval set, never a leaderboard.

check.q: What does continuous batching trade away for higher throughput?
opts: A little speed for each user
Answer accuracy
Prompt caching
check.why: Sharing each weight read across many requests raises throughput, while each request decodes a bit slower.

work: Ask your serving team what batch size limit they run.
Compare a quantized model with the original on your eval set.

reels.title: Retries, fallbacks and budgets

beats.say: The provider says too many requests. Should you retry? Once.
A rate limit is often brief, so one retry with a short wait is fair. Retrying forever turns a hiccup into a storm and a bill.

show.title: Retry rules
items: One retry on a rate limit

beats.say: On an outage or timeout, the gateway falls back to another model that has passed the same evals. An untested fallback just fails differently.
And a daily budget per team, with an alert at eighty percent, catches the agent stuck in a loop before the weekend does.

check.q: A provider has an outage. What should the gateway do?
opts: Fall back to a model that passed the same evals
Retry the same call until it works
Return an error to every user at once
check.why: A tested fallback keeps the feature up; endless retries add load and cost.

work: Check whether your fallback model was ever run against your eval set.
Set a per-team daily budget alert.

reels.title: Gateway or not, API or self-host?

beats.say: Does every company need an LLM gateway and its own GPUs? No.
One team, one model, a small bill: a client library with retries is enough. A gateway pays off when many teams share providers, budgets and data rules.
Use an API until something forces a change: high steady volume where busy GPUs are cheaper, data that cannot leave your network, or a fine-tuned open model.

chip.text: Move only for volume or data rules

beats.say: Self-hosting means owning GPU capacity, batching, quantization choices, upgrades and the pager. Price the people, not just the GPUs.

check.q: Which is the strongest reason to self-host a model?
opts: Data that may not leave your own network
Wanting a faster first prototype
A team of two calling one model
check.why: Data residency is a hard requirement; the other two are better served by an API.

work: Write down which of your AI data may not leave your network.
Estimate GPU cost against your current API bill at steady volume.

reels.title: Owning the gateway, and how it fails

beats.say: Who owns the gateway, and who owns the prompts? Get this wrong and it becomes a bottleneck.
A platform team owns the gateway, provider contracts, quotas and the eval gate for new models. Feature teams own their prompts, eval sets and quality.
It fails as provider outages, timeouts on long prompts, cost spikes from loops, quiet quality drops after a model update, and a gateway that adds latency or goes down itself.

show.title: Watch for
items: The gateway as a single point

beats.say: Move off it when the provider's own gateway covers every model you use, or when one feature's volume earns dedicated serving.

show.title: Move off when
items: One feature needs its own path

check.q: Which should stay with the feature team, not the gateway?
opts: The prompt and its eval set
Quotas and budgets
Provider keys
check.why: Cross-cutting rules live in the gateway; a gateway that edits prompts becomes everyone's bottleneck.

work: Decide who approves a new model before any team can use it.
Make cost per feature visible to each team monthly.
Add a health check and a second instance for the gateway.
